text:
1750 to 1850 was a fascinating period in Indian history.   For over 100 years, European companies (think Coca Cola or Tesla) had profitably  imported spices and textile from India. The looting of the Mughal treasury in 1739 by the Iranian Nader Shah, fragmented the Mughal empire. These fragments  jostled for power and made India unstable and unsafe. To safeguard their warehouses, profits, and trade against this rising instability, European companies raised private armies staffed by Indian sepoys. By a stroke of historical contingency, these corporate forces briefly became more powerful than those of the local kingdoms. Between 1750 and 1775, a narrow window opened: modern military techniques—specifically drilled infantry and the flintlock—had become standard in European warfare but were not yet widespread in India. These private companies saw an opportunity and leveraged this military advantage to run a protection racket with the Carnatic Wars being an excellent example. This tactical dominance soon escalated from influence to outright conquest; after the Battle of Plassey and the Battle of Buxar, they ended up annexing the richest province in the world: Bengal.   Owning Bengal provided a durable advantage even when the Indian kingdoms (e.g., Marathas, Mysore) closed the military map by 1775. With the wealth of Bengal serving as collateral, the European company gained a decisive financing edge; Indian bankers and financiers increasingly backed the Company over local sovereigns. This superior liquidity allowed the Company to maintain larger, better-paid armies that local powers simply could not match. I use the European and not British because it was sheer chance that it was the British East India company and not the French or Dutch who ended up occupying India.

Our collection focuses on coins issued during 1600-1947. It all started when my Dhruvan showed interested in collecting coins. I  ended  up running with it. This website has been a collaborative effort between Claude, Dhruvan and I.
 
- Ram
